reasons: Lake record is verified and identifies the case as Simmons v. United States, decided by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1968.
Official citation is 390 U.S. 377; parallel citations are 88 S. Ct. 967 and 19 L. Ed. 2d 1247; vendor-neutral citation is 1968 U.S. LEXIS 2167.

defect.evidence_quote: We therefore hold that when a defendant testifies in support of a motion to suppress evidence on Fourth Amendment grounds, his testimony may not thereafter be admitted against him at trial on the issue of guilt unless he makes no objection.
defect.problem: The core two-part holding is supported, but the holding summary is slightly overbroad because it omits the Court's explicit no-objection exception for suppression-hearing testimony and compresses the photo-identification rule from setting aside convictions to declaring when the procedure violates due process.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise to: "Convictions based on eyewitness identification at trial following a pretrial photographic identification are set aside only if the photographic procedure was so impermissibly suggestive as to create a very substantial likelihood of irreparable misidentification; and testimony a defendant gives in support of a Fourth Amendment suppression motion may not be admitted against him at trial on guilt unless he makes no objection."

reasons: The photo-identification rule is supported by the opinion text at *384: convictions are set aside only if the photographic procedure was so impermissibly suggestive as to create a very substantial likelihood of irreparable misidentification.
The suppression-hearing testimony rule is supported by the opinion text at *394, but the assertion should carry the Court's express "unless he makes no objection" qualifier.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Carry the exact no-objection qualifier in the short holding.

reasons: The opinion directly announces a due-process standard for eyewitness identification following pretrial photographic identification.

reasons: The opinion frames Garrett's testimony as necessary to establish Fourth Amendment standing to suppress the suitcase evidence.
